opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a strange time. When MIT sent everyone home in March, I was suddenly taking classes over Zoom across a big time difference, so lectures sometimes landed in the middle of the night. Early on I tried to keep my schedule exactly as it had been on campus, and that didn't really work. So I changed my approach.

I leaned much more on self-study. For math especially, I realized a lot of the learning was happening in the problem sets and in working through textbooks myself, not in the live lecture. So I watched recordings when I could actually focus, and I spent most of my energy reading ahead and working problems. In a way, being off campus pushed me to become a more independent learner, and I think that ended up shaping how I approached research later.

The other part was staying connected. On campus you get a lot from just running into people in the hallway or at the problem set sessions. Remotely, you have to be deliberate about it. I set up regular calls with classmates to work through problems together, and I emailed professors more than I would have otherwise. A few of those conversations turned into real mentoring relationships, and some led to research projects. People were surprisingly open, maybe because everyone was isolated and wanted that connection too.

So it was hard, and I definitely missed the campus energy, but it taught me how to structure my own learning and to reach out instead of waiting for opportunities to come to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifting to self-study, watching recordings, working problems, and reaching out to classmates and professors. It does not say she learned to enjoy the difficulty of the coursework itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that moment was pretty disorienting. I was a first-year at MIT, I'd just started to feel like I had a rhythm, and then within about a week we were told to pack up and leave. I flew back home to Guangzhou, and suddenly all my classes were happening in the middle of the night for me because of the twelve-hour time difference.

So the first thing I had to figure out was just logistics. I remember doing a problem set session at three in the morning, and the professor would be very cheerful because for them it was afternoon. I basically flipped my schedule for a while. I'd sleep in the day, wake up in the evening, and work through the night. My parents thought I was a little crazy.

But the more important shift was mental. On campus, so much of the learning happens through osmosis, right? You walk into the math lounge, somebody's at the blackboard, you overhear a conversation and you learn something. That all disappeared. So I had to become much more intentional. I started scheduling calls with classmates just to work on problems together, even if we had nothing specific to discuss. I started reading ahead instead of relying on lecture to pull me along. And I actually reached out to professors more during that time than I had when I was physically there, because the barrier of walking into someone's office was replaced by just sending an email and getting a Zoom link.

In a strange way it made me more independent. I think a lot of people lost motivation that semester, and I understand why. But for me it was the first time I had to really ask myself, do I actually want to learn this, or was I just doing it because I was in the building? And the answer was yes, I wanted to learn it. That clarity ended up being useful later, when I was deciding what to focus on.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes adjusting her schedule, studying intentionally, and becoming more independent, but does not say she learned to enjoy the difficulty of the coursework itself.

astra-6.text: I tried to keep some structure around my classes, even though the setting had changed completely. Without the rhythm of being on campus, I had to be more intentional about setting aside time to study and staying engaged. It was an adjustment, and I took it one week at a time.

r001.rationale: The response describes creating structure, setting aside study time, and staying engaged, but does not present finding enjoyment in the difficulty of the coursework as the approach.

sol-6.1.text: When everyone was sent home, I had to figure out how to keep some structure around my classes. I tried to follow the lectures, stay on top of the assignments, and keep in touch with people so that studying didn’t become completely solitary. It took some adjustment, but having coursework to focus on helped give my days a rhythm.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes maintaining structure, following lectures, completing assignments, and staying connected. It does not say she learned to enjoy the difficulty of the coursework.
